newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Jobless rise puts Bonn EMU forecasts in doubt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Jobless rise puts Bonn EMU forecasts in doubt.

text.p: A rise in German unemployment in May cast doubt over the government's optimistic economic forecasts that are crucial to its plan to qualify for European monetary union, analysts said on Friday.

After releasing figures showing May's seasonally adjusted jobless total rose 56,000 to 4.358 million, the Federal Labour Office chief said he could no longer endorse Bonn's unemployment forecast for this year.
The labour office based its unemployment projections for 1997 on an assumption of 2.25 percent economic gorwth -- below Bonn's official forecast of 2.5 percent.
"I believe the target figure of 3.95 million (average) jobless for 1997 is no longer attainable," Jagoda told a news conference.
He said the economy was not growing fast enough to revive Germany's employment prospects, while Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing called the jobs data "more than disappointing"..
"The seasonal revival in the German jobs market stopped in May. As before the driving forces of the economy are insufficient to bring about a turnaround in the jobs market," Jagoda said.

Based on data from the first five months of the year, and an assumption of 2.25 percent economic growth, average unemployment could climb as high as 4.29 million, said Gerhard Kleinhenz, head of the labour office's research institute.
Higher unemployment would force Bonn to spend more than expected on jobless benefits at a time when it already expects an 18 billion mark ($10.4 billion) shortfall in tax revenue.

The yawning deficit has forced Finance Minister Theo Waigel to scramble for new sources of revenue and precipitated an embarrassing clash with the Bundesbank about booking profits from a revaluation of Germany's gold and currency reserves.

"It is now increasingly clear that Theo Waigel will be unable to bring Germany's budget deficit down to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product this year," HSBC James Capel economist Stephen James said in a research note.
To qualify for the start of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, member nations are supposed to have total public deficits of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
May's unemployment rise did not fit the hoped-for growth scenario for the economy, said Ulrich Beckmann, a senior economist at Deutsche Bank Research in Frankfurt. "This is bad news for Mr. Waigel."
While figures adjusted for seasonal factors rose, unadjusted unemployment fell by 91,000 to 4.256 million.
The unemployment rate published by the Bundesbank based on adjusted data was 11.4 percent in May, compared with 11.2 percent in April.
West German adjusted unemployment rose by 25,000 to 3.042 million. The adjusted unemployment rate in west Germany was 9.9 percent, compared with 9.8 percent a month ago.
In former communist east Germany, the adjusted jobless total increased by 30,000 to 1.316 million, and its adjusted unemployment rate was 17.5, up from 17.1 percent in April.
